newsitem.title: ITALY: Financier Parretti back home to face Italian probe.
newsitem.headline: Financier Parretti back home to face Italian probe.

text.p: Flamboyant financier Giancarlo Parretti, who had apparently fled the U.S. to avoid a court sentence, was forced to return home to face a separate probe in Italy, his lawyer said on Saturday.

The lawyer, Manlio Morcella, told reporters in Parretti's hometown of Orvieto the former chief of the Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer film studio had to return to Italy to face an investigation into alleged tax fraud.

He said Parretti and Delaware judges had reached an agreement which allowed the financier to leave the U.S. and prohibited American judges from sentencing him if legal action against him was also being carried out by Italian judges.
"Parretti had to return to Italy because it was required by the appeals court of Perugia, where he must respond to (alleged) tax crimes for Italian matters," Morcella said.
"He is at peace with himself because his return showed deference to the Italian state," he added.

Parretti was reported to be at his family home in Orvieto, where he was raised on an olive farm before charming his way to an opulent lifestyle and control over MGM, one of Hollywood's most prestigious studios.
An arrest warrant was issued against Parretti in Delaware on Friday after he had apparently fled the U.S.
A Delaware court had been due to sentence him after he was found guilty last October on charges of evidence tampering and perjury, which carry a sentence of up to 10 years.

Parretti was indicted in 1992 on charges he altered documents and lied about it in a Delaware civil trial over his ouster from MGM by the French bank, Credit Lyonnais, whose subsidiary had lent him the money to buy the company.
He had returned voluntarily from Italy to face trial and had been free on bail and living in California.
His lawyer said an Italian Justice Ministry decree would allow Parretti to be sent back to the U.S. "only when the needs of the Italian judges' have been satisfied -- and that has not yet happened".
He also said that Parretti could not be held guilty of perjury "considering the principle of reciprocity and the fact that that crime is not on Italian law books".

Parretti bought MGM in 1991 for $1.3 billion from financier Kirk Kerkorian, who returned to the studio in July 1996 as part of a management-led buyout from a French state-owned holding company formed to dispose of assets of troubled Credit Lyonnais.
